instruction: When do I get breakfast?
response: Breakfast at Children's Hospital comes between 7:45 a.m. and 8:45 a.m. A grown-up on your care team will make sure you get a yummy meal! Sometimes the doctors need you to wait before eating, so your nurse will let you know if that's the case.

instruction: What time is lunch?
response: Lunch arrives between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m. You'll get a menu form on your breakfast tray so you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a restaurant! If you have a question about what foods you can have, your nurse can help.

instruction: When is dinner served here?
response: Dinner time at the hospital is between 4:45 p.m. and 5:45 p.m. That might feel a little earlier than dinner at home, but it gives you plenty of time to enjoy your meal and relax for the evening.

instruction: Can my mom stay with me overnight?
response: Yes! Most patient rooms have a spot where a parent or caregiver can sleep right next to you. There will be clean sheets, pillows, and blankets for them. Your mom just needs to stay in your room during the nighttime hours — between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m. — and let the nurses know she's there.

instruction: Can both my parents visit me?
response: You can have up to two care partners at your bedside at the same time when you're staying overnight. So both your parents can be with you! The nurses might ask them to step out for a little while if they need to do something for your care, but they can come right back.

instruction: Can I bring my teddy bear to the hospital?
response: Absolutely! Bringing a favourite toy or stuffed animal from home can help you feel more comfortable. Just make sure it's clean before you bring it, and try not to share it with other kids in the hospital. Toys that can be wiped down or washed are the best kind to bring.

instruction: Can I bring my tablet?
response: You can bring your tablet! The hospital even has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free, or log in to your own streaming services if you have an account. You can also use the hospital's WiFi to stay connected.

instruction: Why do I have to wear this bracelet?
response: That bracelet is your special hospital armband! It has your name, your birthday, and a barcode on it. Every time a nurse or doctor gives you medicine or does a test, they check your bracelet to make sure they're helping the right person. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe.

instruction: Why does the nurse keep asking me my name?
response: I know it might seem silly when they already know you, but checking your name and birthday is one of the most important safety rules in the hospital. They do it before giving medicine, doing tests, or taking you somewhere — it's how they make double sure everything is right. You're helping keep yourself safe every time you answer!

instruction: Can I bring balloons?
response: Regular latex balloons aren't allowed at Children's Hospital because some people are really allergic to the latex they're made from. But mylar balloons — the shiny, foil kind — are okay! So if someone wants to bring you a balloon, just make sure it's a foil one.

instruction: Can someone bring me flowers?
response: Flowers can be delivered to the hospital by a florist, and there's even a Garden Shoppe at Victoria Hospital where people can buy them. But some hospital units don't allow flowers, so it's a good idea to ask your nurse first. And one special rule — poinsettias are never allowed because they can cause allergic reactions.

instruction: Why can't I bring my perfume?
response: Children's Hospital is a fragrance-free place. That means no perfume, scented lotion, or anything with a strong smell. Some people in the hospital could have trouble breathing or get an allergic reaction from those scents. It's a way of keeping everyone safe and comfortable!

instruction: Why do I have to wash my hands so much?
response: Great question! Washing your hands is the number one best way to stop germs from spreading around the hospital. You should wash them when you go into a patient room, when you leave, and at the end of a visit. You can use soap and water or the hand sanitizer dispensers you'll see around the hospital.

instruction: Is there a playroom here?
response: Yes, there are some really cool spaces to play! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (B6-065) has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. It's open during the day, Monday through Saturday. There's also Ashley's Backyard (B6-259), which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids to relax and play with a grown-up.

instruction: Can I play with the toys in the playroom?
response: Yes! The activity rooms are there for you to enjoy. The School-Age Activity Room has board games, puzzles, LEGO, and crafts. Child Life staff and volunteers also plan fun activities and special events there during the month. Just make sure a grown-up knows where you are when you go.

instruction: What is the SMILE room?
response: The SMILE Room is a really special room on the sixth floor (B6-261). It's filled with cool sensory stuff — like bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help you relax or have fun exploring different sights and sounds. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you can visit!

instruction: Can I watch TV?
response: Yes! The hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If your family has a streaming account — like Netflix or Disney+ — you can log in to that too. Ask your nurse or a staff member if you need help getting it set up.

instruction: Can I use my phone here?
response: Yes, you can use your own cell phone to make calls and stay in touch with family and friends. The hospital has WiFi so you can connect to the internet too. There are also patient telephones you can use for local and toll-free calls at no cost.

instruction: Can my friend come visit me?
response: Friends can visit you at the hospital! Visiting depends on what unit you're on and how you're feeling, so it's a good idea for your parent to check with the nurses about the best time. And remember — your friend shouldn't come if they're feeling sick, because we need to keep everyone in the hospital healthy.

instruction: Why can't my friend come when they have a cold?
response: When someone is sick — even with just a cold — they can spread germs to the kids in the hospital who are already not feeling well. The hospital asks that anyone who is sick or has been feeling sick in the last week not visit. It's a really important rule to protect you and all the other kids here.

instruction: Where can my mom get food?
response: There's a place called On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, in the main atrium. It's open on weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., but it's closed on weekends and holidays. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors.

instruction: Can I eat snacks from home?
response: You might be able to, but you need to check with your care team first. Sometimes the doctors need you on a special diet, or there might be medical reasons you can't eat certain things. If your food is approved, your family can store it in the family fridge — just make sure to put your name and the date on it!

instruction: Do I get to pick my food?
response: Yes! You'll get a form on your breakfast tray where you can choose what you'd like to eat the next day. It's like a little menu. The choices will be based on what your doctor says is okay for you to eat. If you have a food allergy or something you can't eat, let your nurse know and they'll make sure your meals are safe.

instruction: What clothes should I bring?
response: Bring your own comfy clothes, plus slippers or shoes with non-slip bottoms, and an outfit to wear when you go home. Non-slip socks or slippers are really important so you don't slip on the hospital floors. Your parent can also bring your favourite pajamas to help you feel cozy!

instruction: Can I bring my baby walker?
response: Baby walkers aren't allowed at the hospital. This is to keep everyone safe. If you need help walking or moving around, the hospital team has special equipment that's designed just for that. Your nurse can tell you more!

instruction: What should I NOT bring to the hospital?
response: There are a few things to leave at home: latex balloons, baby walkers, small toys that could be swallowed, electrical equipment you bring from home, and anything with perfume or a strong smell. This keeps you and all the other kids safe!

instruction: Why do the nurses come check on me at night?
response: Even when you're fast asleep, a nurse will come by to check on you during the night. They do this to make sure you're comfortable, safe, and that everything is going well. They'll be as quiet as they can so they don't wake you up. It's just their way of taking care of you, even while you're dreaming!

instruction: Why does my bed have rails?
response: The rails on your bed are there to keep you safe so you don't accidentally roll out while you're sleeping or resting. When your parent steps away, they'll put the rails up. If you need to get out of bed, just press the nurse call button and someone will come help you.

instruction: Can I get out of bed by myself?
response: It's safest to ask for help before getting out of bed. Just press the call button and a nurse will come to you. This is because the floors can be slippery and you might be a bit wobbly. Make sure you're wearing your non-slip socks or slippers too!

instruction: How does my room number work?
response: Hospital room numbers are like a little code! If your room is B2-503, here's what it means: the 'B' is the zone (like a section of the hospital), the '2' is the floor number, and '503' is your room. So B2-503 means room 503 on the second floor of Zone B. Pretty cool, right?

instruction: What if I get lost in the hospital?
response: If you ever feel lost, look for an Information Desk — they're open from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays, and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. You can also ask any staff member or volunteer wearing a hospital badge. There are friendly guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. who love to help!

instruction: Is there a quiet place I can go?
response: Yes! There's a place called the Sanctuary on the 3rd floor of Zone C (room C3-402). It's a calm, peaceful space where anyone can go for quiet time. It's open all day and all night, every day. There are also quiet rooms on the sixth floor (B6-119 and B6-257) — just ask your nurse before using them.

instruction: Where is the hospital?
response: Children's Hospital is at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site. If you're coming by car, the closest parking is Parking Lot 8, which is a big garage off Baseline Road.

instruction: Can I bring my LEGO to the hospital?
response: Yes, you can bring LEGO from home! Just try not to bring too many pieces, because keeping your room tidy helps the nurses take care of you. Make sure your LEGO pieces are clean, and remember not to share them with other kids in the hospital. There's also LEGO in the School-Age Activity Room if you want even more building fun!

instruction: Where does my parent sleep?
response: Most rooms have a special spot where your parent can sleep right next to you. They'll get clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. But the rule is that your parent sleeps in their own spot and you sleep in your hospital bed — that way the nurses can reach you easily if they need to.

instruction: Can my little brother visit?
response: Your little brother can come visit! The hospital just asks that visitors check with the nurses about the best time to come, and that he doesn't visit if he's been feeling sick in the past week. An adult should be with him the whole time, and everyone should wash their hands when they come in and when they leave.

instruction: What happens when the nurses change shifts?
response: When one nurse's shift is ending and a new nurse is starting, they do something called a bedside shift change. The new nurse will come to your room and introduce themselves. The two nurses will talk about how you're doing and what your care plan is. Your parent is invited to listen, ask questions, and share anything they think is important. It only takes about three to five minutes!

instruction: Can I bring books from home?
response: Yes! Bringing books from home is a great idea. They can help you feel more comfortable and give you something fun to do. Just make sure they're clean, and try not to share them with other patients. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on the 1st floor of Zone B also has information you can look at.

instruction: What if I need a toothbrush?
response: If you forgot your toothbrush or need other things like deodorant or shampoo, you can get them at the Paediatric Family Resource Centre, the Ronald McDonald Room, or one of the gift shops in the hospital. Just ask your nurse where to find them!

instruction: Is there a place my family can hang out together?
response: Yes! The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a space where patients on the B6 inpatient unit can relax and spend time with family or friends. Sometimes they have special group events and family coffee hours there too. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre on the 1st floor of Zone B.

instruction: Can I bring my pet to visit?
response: Pets from home usually aren't allowed to visit the hospital, because it's important to keep all the patients, visitors, and staff safe and healthy. But in very special cases, a pet visit might be allowed with permission from the unit manager. There are also therapy dogs that visit sometimes — ask your care team if there's a therapy dog visit coming up!

instruction: Can a therapy dog come see me?
response: Children's Hospital works with St. John Ambulance to have therapy dogs visit certain units! These are specially trained dogs that come to help kids feel better. Ask your nurse or someone on your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up — it's a really special treat.

instruction: Why does someone walk into my room without knocking at night?
response: That's one of your nurses doing a nighttime check! During your whole stay, a nurse will come by regularly — even at night — to make sure you're safe and comfortable. They try to be very quiet so they don't wake you up. It's part of how they take good care of you around the clock.

instruction: Can my grandma bring homemade cookies?
response: That's sweet of your grandma! But before you eat anything that's brought from home, you need to check with your care team first. Sometimes kids in the hospital have to be on a special diet or can't eat certain things for medical reasons. If the team says it's okay, you can enjoy them! Just make sure to put any leftovers in the family fridge with your name and the date on them.

instruction: What if my mom needs to leave for a bit?
response: It's okay if your mom needs to step away for a little while. She just needs to let the nurse know so they can keep an extra close eye on you. Before she goes, she'll make sure the rails on your bed or crib are up and that only safe things are within your reach. She can also ask security to walk her to her car if it's dark outside by calling extension 52281.

instruction: Can I bring my Nintendo Switch?
response: You can bring a handheld gaming device like that! Just make sure you're careful with it and don't share it with other patients. The hospital also has WiFi so you can connect online. You're not allowed to bring big electrical equipment from home, but handheld gaming devices are fine.

instruction: What is the red bracelet for?
response: If you have any allergies, you'll be given a special red bracelet. This bracelet tells everyone on your care team — nurses, doctors, and other helpers — about your allergies so they can keep you extra safe. It's like a little alert signal that everyone can see!

instruction: Where can I find snacks on the floor?
response: If you're staying on the B6 inpatient unit, there are pantries in rooms B6-149 and B6-231 that have drinks and light snacks for patients. If you're at the Paediatric Medical Day Unit, they also provide light snacks for kids during day treatment. Just ask your nurse what's available!

instruction: What do I need to bring for my appointment?
response: For your appointment, your parent should bring your Ontario health card, your appointment card or letter, any medicine you're taking, your family doctor's name and phone number, and any medical papers like X-rays or referral letters. You can bring a favourite book or toy to keep you busy while you wait!

instruction: Can I sleep in my mom's bed in the hospital?
response: Each kid needs to sleep in their own hospital bed or crib. This is so the nurses can reach you easily if they need to check on you or help you. Your mom will have her own sleeping spot right nearby, so she'll still be super close.

instruction: Is there an app to find my way around the hospital?
response: Yes! You can download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map. It helps you and your family find your way around. There are also wayfinding kiosks inside the hospital and QR codes on posters near the elevators that you can scan.

instruction: Can I bring my own pillow?
response: Yes, you can bring your own pillow to help you feel more at home! The hospital does provide pillows and blankets, but having your own special one is totally fine. Just make sure it's clean when you bring it in.

instruction: Why do some rooms have signs on the door?
response: Some rooms have special signs when a patient needs extra germ protection. If you see a sign, it means there are extra rules — like wearing gloves, a gown, or a mask before going in. It's nothing scary, it's just to keep germs from spreading. If you see a sign on someone's room, stop at the nurses' station first and they'll tell you what to do.

instruction: What is the family fridge for?
response: The family fridge is where your family can store food they bring from home. It even has a freezer! Just make sure to write your name and the date on everything. The hospital isn't responsible if someone accidentally takes your food, so labels really help. Check with your care team before eating anything that's brought in.

instruction: Can I walk around the hospital?
response: You might be able to, depending on how you're feeling and what your care team says. Some kids need to stay in their room or bed, especially if there are infection control rules. Always ask your nurse before going for a walk, and make sure you wear non-slip socks or shoes so you don't slip!

instruction: What if I don't like the food?
response: If you don't enjoy what you get, let your nurse know! The hospital offers different kinds of diets and they really try to give you things you'll like. You get to pick your meals on a form that comes with your breakfast tray. If something doesn't taste good to you, it's totally okay to speak up.

instruction: Can my family bring me a birthday cake?
response: That's a nice idea! But before anyone brings food from outside, your care team needs to check if it's safe for you to eat. Some kids are on special diets or have allergies. Ask your nurse first, and if they say yes, you can celebrate! Just remember the hospital is fragrance-free, so no scented candles.

instruction: Where do I go when I first get to the hospital?
response: When you arrive, you'll go to Patient Registration on the second floor of Zone B, which is above the main entrance. That's where they'll get you checked in. If you need help finding it, there are guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays who can show you the way!

instruction: Can I use the bathroom in another kid's room?
response: No, visitors should use a different bathroom, not the one in a patient's room. This is to help stop germs from spreading between patients. Your nurse can tell you where the closest bathroom for visitors is.

instruction: What are the Bravery Beads?
response: Bravery Beads are a really cool program! Each bead represents something you've been through in the hospital — like a test, a treatment, or a brave moment. You collect them to make a special necklace or string that tells YOUR unique story. Kids of all ages can join the program if they want — it's totally voluntary.

instruction: When does the front door lock?
response: The main entrance to Children's Hospital (the B Tower entrance) is open from 6:00 in the morning until 8:30 at night. After that, you need to check in with the security guard to get inside. If your parent is coming through the parking garage, that entrance is open 24 hours, but they still need to check in with security after hours.

instruction: Can my family eat in my room?
response: Your family can be with you during your meals! If they want to get their own food, there's Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B (open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.) and vending machines on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B near the elevators. They can also store food in the family fridge.

instruction: Can I bring family photos?
response: Yes! Bringing a few family pictures is a great idea — they can help your room feel more like home and make you feel less homesick. Just try not to bring too many things, because keeping your space tidy helps the nurses take good care of you.

instruction: What does the hand sanitizer do?
response: The hand sanitizer — also called alcohol-based hand rub — kills the germs on your hands really quickly. It's the best way to clean your hands when they don't look dirty. You'll see dispensers all around the hospital, and everyone — doctors, nurses, visitors, and you — should use them before entering and leaving patient rooms!

instruction: Can I bring too many toys?
response: It's best to bring just a few favourites rather than a whole bunch. Too many things in your room can create clutter, and that makes it harder for the nurses and doctors to take care of you. If you have too much stuff, some of it might need to go home with a visitor. A couple of special things is just right!

instruction: Where is the pharmacy?
response: The Children's Hospital Pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 Entrance — the room is B1-001. It's open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. (it's closed on holidays). If your doctor gives you a prescription, your family can fill it here before you leave!

instruction: Can someone pray at the hospital?
response: Yes! There's a special place called the Sanctuary on the 3rd floor of Zone C (room C3-402). It's open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and everyone is welcome. It's a quiet space for praying, thinking, or just having a peaceful moment. If your family would like to talk to a Spiritual Care Specialist, your nurse can help.

instruction: Do I have to stay in my room the whole time?
response: Not always! Depending on how you're feeling and what your doctors say, you might be able to visit the playrooms, family spaces, or other areas. But always check with your nurse first — sometimes there are rules about staying in your room, especially if you need extra germ protection.

instruction: What if my parent doesn't speak English?
response: The hospital offers free interpreter services so your parent can talk to the doctors and nurses in the language they're most comfortable with. Your care team can arrange for an interpreter. Everyone deserves to understand what's happening, and the hospital wants to make sure your family does.

instruction: Where is the garden?
response: There's a beautiful garden called Alex's Butterfly Garden on Level 2 of Zone D. It's a quiet, peaceful outdoor space with benches and a water fountain. Kids, families, and staff can all go there to enjoy some fresh air and quiet time.

instruction: Why does my nurse check my bracelet before everything?
response: Your nurse checks your bracelet every single time before giving you medicine, doing a test, or taking you somewhere. It has your name, birthday, and a special barcode on it. They scan it or read it to make absolutely sure they're giving the right thing to the right kid. It's one of the most important safety rules!

instruction: Can I bring my glasses to the hospital?
response: You should definitely bring your glasses! The hospital guide says to bring any important medical aids like eyeglasses, hearing aids, braces, or crutches. You need to be able to see clearly, so don't forget to pack them.

instruction: Can my teacher visit me?
response: Your teacher can visit as long as they follow the visitor rules — they should check with the nurses about the best time, wash their hands when they come in and when they leave, and make sure they aren't feeling sick. It's really nice when familiar people come to see you!

instruction: Where can I get a drink of water?
response: Ask your nurse! They can bring you water or let you know where to get it on your unit. On the B6 inpatient floor, there are pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks available. But always check with your care team first, because sometimes the doctors need you to wait before drinking.

instruction: Can I go outside during my stay?
response: That depends on your care plan. Some kids can visit outdoor spaces like Alex's Butterfly Garden. But always ask your nurse before going anywhere outside your room. They'll let you know if it's safe for you to take a little trip outside.

instruction: What happens when I'm ready to leave the hospital?
response: When it's time to go home, your care team will tell you and your parents all about how to take care of you at home — like what medicines you need, what food to eat, and when to come back for a check-up. Make sure to bring a car seat if you need one, and pack up all your things! Your nurse will go over everything before you leave.

instruction: Do I need a car seat to go home?
response: Yes! It's the law that all children must travel in an approved car seat. Make sure your parent brings your car seat when they come to pick you up. The hospital even has a Car Seat Program with special helpers who can make sure your car seat is put in correctly.

instruction: What should I wear home from the hospital?
response: Your parents should bring you a comfy set of clothes for going home! Make sure they bring shoes too. When you find out your discharge day, having your clothes ready will make everything go smoothly.

instruction: Can I take my medicine from home while I'm here?
response: You should bring your medicines with you so the doctors know what you take, but you can't take them at the hospital unless your care team says it's okay. The hospital will give you the medicines you need while you're here. Always let your nurse know about every medicine you take — even vitamins and creams!

instruction: Where are the vending machines?
response: The vending machines are near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors. There are ATMs there too if your parent needs cash. For a bigger meal, there's Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B.

instruction: Can someone walk my mom to the car at night?
response: Yes! If your mom needs to go to her car when it's dark, she can call the Security team at extension 52281 and they'll send someone to walk with her. They can also walk her to the Ronald McDonald House. It's there to help everyone feel safe.

instruction: Why do people keep telling me to use hand gel?
response: The hand gel (hand sanitizer) is the hospital's best tool for fighting germs. Hospitals have to be extra careful about germs because sick kids can catch things more easily. Using hand gel before going into a room and when leaving is one of the most important things everyone can do — including you! It only takes a few seconds.

instruction: What if my bracelet falls off?
response: If your armband comes off, tell your nurse right away! They'll put a new one on for you. That bracelet is really important because it has your name, birthday, and a barcode that they check before giving you any medicine or doing any tests. Don't worry — it happens sometimes, and getting a new one is quick.

instruction: What are the visiting rules if someone in the room next to me is sick?
response: Visiting rules are set up to protect everyone. If someone nearby needs extra germ protection, the nurses might have special instructions — like wearing a mask or gown. If you see a sign outside someone's room, don't go in without checking with a nurse first. And always, always wash your hands!

instruction: Can I use the supply cart in the hallway?
response: The supply carts in the hallway are for the hospital staff to use. Visitors and patients shouldn't touch the things on the carts. If you need something, just ask your nurse and they'll get it for you!

instruction: Can I sit on an empty hospital bed?
response: Even if a bed next to you looks empty, it needs to stay clean for the next child who might need it. So visitors and parents shouldn't sit on, put their feet on, or sleep in empty hospital beds. Your nurse can help find a comfortable chair for your visitors.

instruction: How can I tell my nurse something?
response: You can always talk to your nurse directly, or press the call button near your bed. During bedside shift changes, which happen in the morning and evening, you and your parent are invited to share anything important. Never be afraid to speak up — the nurses want to hear from you!

instruction: Is there an outdoor space to play?
response: There's Alex's Butterfly Garden on Level 2 of Zone D — it has benches and a nice water fountain. It's not exactly a playground, but it's a beautiful, calming outdoor spot where you can enjoy being outside for a little while. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to go!

instruction: What if I spill something in my room?
response: Accidents happen! If you spill something, let your nurse know. The cleaning staff will take care of it to make sure the floor doesn't get slippery. Keeping the floor clean and dry is important to prevent falls.

instruction: Why does the hospital smell funny?
response: The hospital uses special cleaning products to keep everything really clean and germ-free. That clean smell is how you know the hospital is working hard to keep you safe! The hospital is also fragrance-free, which means nobody wears perfume or uses smelly lotions, so the only smell is that clean hospital smell.

instruction: Can I bring my favourite blanket?
response: Yes! Bringing your own blanket is a great idea to help you feel comfortable and cozy. The hospital gives you blankets too, but your special one from home can make things feel a little more normal. Just make sure it's clean when you bring it.

instruction: Can I do arts and crafts here?
response: You sure can! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (B6-065) has crafts you can do, and Child Life staff and volunteers plan special art activities too. There's also an Art Therapy program that helps kids express their feelings through art. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about what's available!

instruction: What if I need something from the store?
response: There are gift shops at the hospital where your family can buy things you might need. The pharmacy at B1-001 is open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Victoria's Place is at the B1 entrance. Your nurse can point your family in the right direction.

instruction: What are meal times at Children's Hospital?
response: Meals at Children's Hospital are served at set times each day. Breakfast is between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch runs from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m., and dinner is served from 4:45 to 5:45 p.m. You'll receive a menu form with your breakfast tray to select your meals for the following day. If you have dietary restrictions or allergies, let your care team know — they accommodate vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, and allergen-specific diets.

instruction: What time is breakfast here?
response: Breakfast is served between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m. You'll get a form on your breakfast tray to choose what you want to eat the next day. If you have any food allergies or dietary needs — like halal, kosher, vegan, or allergen-free — make sure your care team knows so they can set up the right menu for you.

instruction: When's lunch?
response: Lunch is from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. You pick your meals ahead of time on a form that comes with breakfast. Before you eat anything — including food people bring you from outside — always check with your care team. There could be dietary restrictions tied to your treatment.

instruction: Can my parents both stay with me?
response: If you're an inpatient, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at the same time. For outpatient visits, it's one care partner per patient. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., whoever is staying with you overnight should remain in your room and let the unit staff know they're there.

instruction: What are the visitor rules?
response: Visiting is based on your condition, care needs, and your wishes, so times may vary between patients and units. Check with the unit staff about optimal visiting times. A few key rules: visitors should not come if they've been sick in the last week, everyone must wash their hands or use hand sanitizer before and after visiting, and visiting may be paused temporarily for care needs or privacy reasons. Overnight visitors (8:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.) should stay in the patient's room.

instruction: How many visitors can I have?
response: For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at one time. The hospital encourages keeping visits manageable — too many visitors at once can be tough when you're trying to rest and recover. If your unit is on outbreak precautions, only essential care partners may be permitted. Check with your care team for specifics.

instruction: What should I bring for my hospital stay?
response: For your stay, bring your own clothes (including slippers with non-slip soles and an outfit for going home), toiletries like toothbrush, shampoo, and deodorant, and any medical aids you use — glasses, hearing aids, braces, etc. A few favourite items from home like books or photos can help. You'll also need your Ontario health card and a list of any medications you take. Leave latex balloons, perfume/fragrances, baby walkers, and electrical equipment at home.

instruction: What shouldn't I bring to the hospital?
response: Leave these at home: latex balloons (they can trigger severe allergies), perfume or any scented products (the hospital is fragrance-free), baby walkers, small items that could be a choking hazard for younger patients, and personal electrical equipment. The hospital takes these rules seriously to protect all patients.

instruction: Is there WiFi?
response: Yes, the hospital has WiFi available for patients. You can connect your phone, tablet, or laptop. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming services. If you need help with WiFi, you can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958.

instruction: Can I use my phone in the hospital?
response: Absolutely. The hospital encourages patients to use their own cell phones to make calls and keep in touch with people. There's WiFi for internet access, and patient telephones are also available for free local and toll-free calls. So staying connected with friends and family shouldn't be a problem.

instruction: Where can I grab food?
response: On the Go featuring Tim Hortons is on the second floor of Zone B in the main atrium — open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. (closed weekends and holidays). Vending machines and ATMs are near the Zone B elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors. If you're an inpatient on B6, there are pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks. A full list of food options is on the LHSC website.

instruction: Can I eat food people bring me from outside?
response: Check with your care team first. Depending on your condition, you might be on a specific diet or restricted from certain foods. If they clear it, your family can store outside food in the family fridge — just label it with your name and date. The hospital isn't responsible for anything that goes missing from the fridge.

instruction: Do I have to wear the hospital bracelet?
response: Yes, the ID bracelet is a requirement for your safety. It has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode. Staff will check it before administering any medication, performing tests, or taking you for a procedure. If you have allergies, you'll also get a red allergy bracelet. If your bracelet falls off or is damaged, let your nurse know immediately.

instruction: Why do they keep asking me to confirm my name and birthday?
response: It's a standardized patient safety protocol. Before any medication, test, or procedure, staff verify your identity by checking your name and date of birth against your armband. It might feel repetitive, but it's one of the most effective ways to prevent medical errors. If something ever seems off — like a wrong name or medication — speak up. They want you to.

instruction: What's the deal with the fragrance-free rule?
response: LHSC is entirely fragrance-free. That means no perfume, cologne, scented lotion, body spray, or any scented products. Some patients and staff have respiratory conditions or allergies that can be triggered by fragrances, and in a hospital setting where people are already vulnerable, it's an important precaution. Ask anyone visiting you to skip fragrances too.

instruction: Is smoking allowed anywhere on the property?
response: No. LHSC is completely smoke-free — all buildings, grounds, and parking lots. This includes cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, and cannabis. The only exemption is for the traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous Peoples, for which a designated space is provided.

instruction: Can I vape at the hospital?
response: No. Under the Smoke-Free Ontario Act, LHSC is entirely smoke-free — that includes e-cigarettes and vapes. The policy covers all buildings, grounds, and parking lots without exception.

instruction: How does the room numbering work?
response: Room numbers follow the format like B2-503. The letter (B) is the zone, the number right after it (2) is the floor, and the last numbers (503) are the room itself. So B2-503 means room 503 on the 2nd floor of Zone B. It's pretty straightforward once you know the system. You can also use the MazeMap app to navigate.

instruction: Where do I register when I arrive?
response: Patient Registration is on the second floor of Zone B, above the main entrance. Your admitting time is scheduled in relation to your procedure. If you need to find out a patient's room or phone number, you can call the Patient Information Desk at 519-663-3163.

instruction: What time do the doors lock?
response: The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily. After 8:30 p.m., entry is controlled by Security and caregivers need to check in with the guard. The parking garage entrance is open 24 hours, but after hours you still need to check in with Security. Zone D entrances on Levels 2 and 3 lock at 8:00 p.m. and reopen at 6:00 a.m., while Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked 24/7.

instruction: Is there somewhere quiet I can go?
response: There are a few options. The Sanctuary (C3-402) is a sacred space open 24/7 for quiet reflection, meditation, or prayer. On the sixth floor, there are Quiet Rooms at B6-119 and B6-257 — these can be used for private phone calls, short breaks, or family meetings. Just check with your nurse or unit clerk before using the quiet rooms. They're not meant for sleeping.

instruction: Can I bring my own food?
response: You can, but you need to clear it with your care team first. Depending on your treatment, you might be on a prescribed diet. If approved, you can store personal food in the family fridge in your unit's pantry area — label it with your name and date. On B6, pantries are at B6-149 and B6-231. The hospital isn't responsible for food that gets taken from the fridge.

instruction: Where does my parent sleep if they stay?
response: Most inpatient rooms provide a sleep space for one family member with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. In the PCCU, there are two sleep spaces at the bedside plus a nearby quiet room and sleep room. On B6, there's one overnight spot per patient. The NICU has kangaroo and sleeper chairs, though space can be limited. Each child must sleep in their own hospital bed — parents can't share it.

instruction: What about parking?
response: Parking is available 24/7 across several lots. The closest to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, a garage off Baseline Road. It's $4 for the first hour, $2 per half hour after that, with a daily max of $12 (no in-and-out). Multi-day passes are available from the parking office: 7-day for $45, 14-day for $65, or 30-day for $75. You can pay with Visa, Mastercard, or cash. The parking office is in P8, ground floor, Room 105.

instruction: How much does parking cost?
response: It's $4 for the first hour and $2 for each additional half hour, up to a $12 daily maximum without in-and-out privileges. If your family needs to come and go, a daily pass with in-and-out privileges is $14 (valid 24 hours). For longer stays, passes are available: $45 for 7 days, $65 for 14 days, and $75 for 30 days. These are valid at all LHSC sites.

instruction: What if I don't speak English well?
response: LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients. If you're more comfortable communicating in a language other than English, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, ask your care team to arrange an interpreter. You deserve to fully understand your care, and the hospital takes that seriously. They support spoken languages and sign language.

instruction: Can I bring my pet?
response: Family pet visits are generally not permitted to protect the health and safety of patients, visitors, and staff. Service animals are the exception. In very rare compassionate cases, a pet visit might be approved by the unit manager, but it requires proof of vaccination and a signed waiver. The hospital also has a therapy dog program through St. John Ambulance — ask your care team about scheduled visits.

instruction: What are the hand hygiene rules?
response: Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to prevent infections in the hospital. You should clean your hands before entering a patient room, when leaving, and at the end of any visit. Alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method when hands aren't visibly soiled. If they are, use soap and water. Hand sanitizer dispensers are throughout the hospital. It applies to everyone — patients, families, staff.

instruction: What infection control rules should I know about?
response: Key rules: wash or sanitize your hands frequently, don't visit if you're feeling unwell or have been sick in the past week, don't sit on hospital beds or chairs covered with sheets, don't use patient washrooms if you're a visitor, and don't touch supplies on the carts — ask staff instead. Some patients may require extra precautions like gowns, gloves, or masks. If you see a sign posted outside a room, check with the nurses' station before entering.

instruction: What happens during the bedside shift change?
response: At shift change, the outgoing and incoming nurses meet at your bedside for about three to five minutes. The new nurse introduces themselves, they review your care plan, complete mandatory safety checks, and ask if you or your family have questions or anything to add. You're encouraged to participate — it's your care, and your input matters. Nursing shift changes happen daily around 6:45–7:30 a.m. and 6:45–7:30 p.m.

instruction: What time do nurse shift changes happen?
response: Nursing shift changes happen twice a day, from 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. It's harder to get through to the unit by phone during these times. The bedside shift change report takes about three to five minutes, and you're welcome to be part of it.

instruction: Where is the pharmacy?
response: The Children's Hospital Pharmacy and Compounding Centre is at B1-001, on the first floor of Children's Hospital next to the B1 Entrance. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. (closed on holidays). You can fill prescriptions there before discharge.

instruction: Can I take my own meds while I'm admitted?
response: Bring your medications or a complete list of them (including over-the-counter, herbal products, vitamins, creams, inhalers, and eye drops), but don't take anything from home unless your care team explicitly approves it. While admitted, the hospital will supply any medications prescribed for use at LHSC. Let your nurse and physician know about any recently stopped medications and any allergies.

instruction: What do I need to know about going home?
response: Before discharge, your care team will review everything — medications, care instructions, diet, follow-up appointments. Make sure you understand dosages, side effects, and who to call if something goes wrong. Have your ride arranged in advance and bring a car seat if required by law. If you need home care equipment, it has to be assessed by an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator before you leave. Ask for written instructions so you have everything in hand.

instruction: How do I prepare to leave the hospital?
response: Your care team starts planning for discharge early in your stay. Before you leave, you'll go over your medications (purpose, dosage, side effects, next dose timing), any equipment needs, follow-up appointment schedules, and any activity or dietary changes at home. Make sure you know who to contact in an emergency. Pack up all your belongings, confirm your ride, and bring a car seat if needed. If you've been here more than 14 days with existing community services, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required.

instruction: What is the Comfort Promise?
response: The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety during needle procedures. They use evidence-based strategies: topical anesthetic to numb the skin, comfort positioning (sitting upright with secure, supportive holds instead of restraint), and distraction techniques like watching videos or playing with something. For infants under 12 months, sucrose and breastfeeding are also used. You're encouraged to ask about these strategies before any needle procedure.

instruction: Can I ask for numbing cream before a needle?
response: Yes — it's actually part of the hospital's Comfort Promise. They offer topical anesthetic (usually a cream or gel) that numbs the skin before needle procedures. It works quickly. You can also ask about comfort positioning and distraction techniques. Don't hesitate to advocate for yourself — the whole point of the Comfort Promise is that you shouldn't have to just tough it out.

instruction: Where is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?
response: It's on the 1st floor of Zone B, room B1-006. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; Tuesday and Thursday from 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.; and Saturday and Sunday from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. by appointment only. They offer peer support, help with forms, and information about children's health from a lived-experience perspective.

instruction: Is there a social worker I can talk to?
response: Yes. Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical help — like information about community resources and financial supports. They can also help with communication between your family and the care team, and with planning for discharge. Ask your nurse or a member of your care team to connect you. The social work line is 519-685-8500, extension 33131.

instruction: What if I have a complaint about my care?
response: Start by talking with your care team directly — they may be able to resolve it right away. If that doesn't work, you can contact Patient Relations by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, or through the online contact form on the LHSC website. They check messages Monday to Friday between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.

instruction: Is there spiritual care available?
response: Yes. LHSC has Spiritual Care Specialists who provide support that's respectful of all spiritual and religious needs, beliefs, and practices. You can reach one through your nurse at pager number 14693 or by calling extension 58418. There's also the Sanctuary in Zone C, Level 3, room C3-402 — it's a sacred space open 24/7 for prayer, reflection, or quiet time.

instruction: Where can I do laundry or get toiletries?
response: If you need personal care items like a toothbrush, deodorant, or shampoo, check the Paediatric Family Resource Centre (B1-006), the Ronald McDonald Room, or the hospital gift shops. As for laundry, the guide doesn't mention on-site laundry facilities for families, so you'd want to ask your care team about local options or have someone bring fresh clothes.

instruction: What's the B6 unit like?
response: B6 is the paediatric inpatient unit. It's a locked unit — once you're admitted, you get a confidential code to enter. There's one overnight sleep space per patient for a family member, with clean bedding provided. The unit has pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks, a family fridge, the Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110), quiet rooms (B6-119 and B6-257), the SMILE Room (B6-261), Ashley's Backyard playroom (B6-259), and the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065).

instruction: What do I do if I see a sign on someone's door?
response: Signs posted at a patient's room or bed space indicate that extra infection control precautions are in effect. Stop at the nurses' station before entering and they'll tell you what's needed — it might mean wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection. A staff member can help you put these on. These measures protect both you and the patient.

instruction: How do I get an interpreter?
response: Ask your care team. LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients, including spoken languages and sign language. If you're more comfortable communicating in a language other than English, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, they'll arrange the right support. A downloadable list of available spoken languages is on the LHSC website.

instruction: Is there a weapons detection system?
response: Yes, in the Emergency Departments. LHSC has a weapons detection system at ED entrances. Everyone entering the ED has to pass through it each time. It uses non-invasive technology — you walk through without stopping or removing personal items. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. If you need accommodations, speak to the security guard at the ED entrance before going through.

instruction: Can I leave the unit during my stay?
response: That depends on your condition and care plan. Always check with your nurse before leaving the unit. If you're on infection precautions, you may need to stay in your room. On the B6 inpatient unit, which is locked, you'll need your confidential code to re-enter. Let your care team know whenever you leave so they know where you are.

instruction: What should I know about privacy here?
response: LHSC takes your privacy seriously. Information about you is only shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent or refuse the collection and use of your personal health information, access your records, request corrections, be notified if your information is accessed inappropriately, and know who it's been shared with. If you have concerns, contact the Privacy Office at 519-685-8500 extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Can I ask for a specific diet?
response: Yes. LHSC offers a range of diets including vegan, vegetarian (with various levels — dairy and eggs, or dairy/eggs/fish), halal, kosher, no pork, and meals free of priority allergens like eggs, milk, nuts, and mustard. Your physician prescribes a diet based on your medical needs, and Patient Food Services creates a menu from there. Talk to your care team to get the right diet set up.

instruction: How can I get around the hospital?
response: You can download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map, use the wayfinding kiosks on-site, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays. Information Desks are open 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby are available weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.

instruction: Where can I park?
response: The closest lot to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, the garage off Baseline Road. Other options include P1 and P2 off Commissioners Road, P3 south of Zone E, and P7 off Baseline Road north of Zone E. All lots are paid, open 24/7. Rates start at $4 for the first hour. The parking office in P8 (ground floor, Room 105) is open Monday to Friday 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.

instruction: Can my friends visit whenever they want?
response: Visiting times aren't fixed hospital-wide — they vary by unit and depend on your condition and care needs. Check with the unit staff about optimal visiting times. Visitors shouldn't come if they've been sick in the past week, and visiting may be interrupted or restricted for your care, privacy, or safety. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., visitors should be in your room and staff should be aware of their presence.

instruction: What's the security situation here?
response: LHSC has security patrols and several access control measures. The B Tower entrance is open 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. and controlled by security after hours. Certain zones lock at 8:00 p.m. or are locked 24/7. The Emergency Department has a weapons detection system. If you need a security escort to your car or the Ronald McDonald House, call dispatch at extension 52281. For emergencies, the extension is 55555.

instruction: Where is the Ronald McDonald House?
response: The Ronald McDonald House is available for families who live outside London. Ask your care team about eligibility and availability. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room within the hospital — you can reach them at 519-685-8500, extension 56896. If you need an escort to the Ronald McDonald House, Security can help — call extension 52281.

instruction: What are the rules about bringing toys and stuff?
response: You can bring personal items to make your stay more comfortable, but keep it reasonable — clutter can interfere with cleaning and safe care, and excess items may be sent home with visitors. Toys should be clean and wipeable/washable. Don't share personal items with other patients to prevent infection spread. Staff may clean or restrict certain items if there are infection control concerns. Leave latex balloons, fragranced items, and small choking-hazard items at home.

instruction: Is there a therapist I can talk to?
response: There are several options. Paediatric Psychology Services offers assessment and treatment for adjustment challenges, coping strategies, and emotional and behavioural support. Social workers provide emotional support and advocacy. Child Life Specialists help with coping and self-expression. There's also Spiritual Care if that's helpful for you. Ask your care team to connect you with whoever fits best.

instruction: What is the Gender Pathways Service?
response: The Gender Pathways Service (GPS) provides gender-affirming care for gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service that follows North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. You can learn more by contacting gps@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Is there Indigenous cultural support available?
response: Yes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant supports mental health and cultural wellness for Indigenous kids at Children's Hospital, bridging traditional ways of knowing with western approaches to healing. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space at E1-204, open to all with priority to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous Peoples. Ask your care team about access or visit the LHSC website for details.

instruction: What's the Black Health Navigator?
response: Black Health Navigators are registered health-care workers who help Black patients and families navigate the health-care system. They provide information about health-care options and make sure your voice is heard in conversations with care teams. You can access this service through Black Health — ask your care team or email BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Can I use Upopolis?
response: If you're between 8 and 18, yes. Upopolis is a free, secure social networking site where paediatric patients can connect with each other across Canada. Laptops are available through Child Life Services for you to use it. Talk to a Child Life Specialist to get set up.

instruction: What is the PCCU like for overnight stays?
response: In the Paediatric Critical Care Unit, there are two sleep spaces right at your bedside for family members, with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets provided. There's also a nearby quiet room that sleeps one and a sleep room that sleeps two — they share a bathroom with a shower. Space is set up to keep family close while giving the care team room to do their work.

instruction: What happens in the Emergency Department if I need to stay overnight?
response: There aren't dedicated sleeping accommodations in the Paediatric Emergency Department. One caregiver should stay with you at all times. Staff will do their best to provide a reclining or fold-out chair, plus pillows and blankets, so you can rest as comfortably as possible. If you end up being admitted, you'll be moved to an inpatient unit with better overnight facilities.

instruction: What if I want to recognize a staff member who was great?
response: LHSC has a Great Moments Recognition Program for exactly that. You can fill out the form on the LHSC website to recognize a staff member, physician, volunteer, learner, or patient partner who made a difference. They'll receive a letter of appreciation and a small item of recognition. If you don't remember their exact name, share as many details as you can to help identify them.

instruction: How can I participate in research?
response: During your stay, your physician or a research team member may discuss studies with you. All clinical research at LHSC is reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Board. Participation is always voluntary — declining won't affect your care. If you're interested, ask your care team about clinical trials or studies that might be a fit. Take your time to read the Letter of Information and ask questions before committing.

instruction: What if I need legal help?
response: Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) has a partnership with Children's Hospital. They provide free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. The program helps identify and resolve legal problems that could impact a child's health or a family's ability to provide care. Your social worker can refer your case to their on-site triage lawyer.

instruction: What is the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program?
response: The PPI program prepares one caregiver to accompany and support you in the operating room during the start of anaesthesia. It includes an education session and/or a tour of Day Surgery and the OR to help you both get ready. Not everyone is eligible, so check with your care team or a Child Life Specialist to see if this is an option for your procedure.

instruction: Where can I do something fun during my stay?
response: There are several spaces: the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO — open daily Monday through Saturday. Ashley's Backyard (B6-259) is a nature-themed playroom. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with bubble columns, fibre optics, and music. The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a social space. There's also art therapy, music therapy, the Heroes' Circle, and Ollie the Clown visiting sometimes.

instruction: What arts and therapeutic programs are available?
response: Quite a few. Art Therapy lets you express thoughts and feelings through creative activities. Music Therapy is provided by an accredited music therapist — no musical skill needed. The Heroes' Circle is a weekly program involving breathing techniques, relaxation, and martial arts. Ollie the therapeutic clown visits to bring play and laughter. And the Bravery Beads program lets you document your journey with beads representing each element of your care.

instruction: What kind of support is there for transitioning between youth and adult care?
response: The Transitions in Care team specifically supports paediatric patients and families through key milestones — like transitioning from youth to adult care, and moving between school and hospital. If you're approaching 18 or nearing a transition point, ask your care team about connecting with them.

instruction: What if there's an emergency on the unit?
response: For any emergency in the hospital, the extension to call is 55555. Security can be reached at extension 52281 for non-emergency safety concerns. If something feels wrong or unsafe during your stay, speak up to your nurse or any staff member immediately.

instruction: Are there charges for anything during my stay?
response: Most of your care is covered, but there may be charges for certain supplies and devices not covered by OHIP — things like crutches, breast pumps, or surgical supplies. The Business Office is in Zone D, 3rd floor, Room D3-400. You'll receive an invoice by mail and can pay online, at the bank, or by cheque. Parking is also a paid service.

instruction: Is there financial help available for families?
response: Social workers can help your family access financial resources and community services. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre offers help with forms and applications. Pro Bono Law Ontario provides free legal assistance for low-income families. Some hotels nearby may offer hospital rates. Ask your care team or social worker — they're there to help navigate these things.

instruction: What happens if I'm on a locked unit?
response: The B6 inpatient unit is locked for patient safety. When you're admitted, you'll receive a confidential code to enter the unit. This isn't meant to feel restrictive — it's a security measure to protect everyone on the floor. Your visitors and family will need to follow the unit's entry procedures too.

instruction: What if my nurse isn't available when someone calls for me?
response: It can be harder to get through to the unit by phone during nursing shift changes, which happen from 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. The hospital suggests having one family member act as the main contact person who can relay updates to everyone else. When calling the unit, provide your full name and ask to speak with your nurse.

instruction: Can I go out to smoke or vape during my stay?
response: No. LHSC is entirely smoke-free — all buildings, grounds, and parking lots. That includes cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, and cannabis. There's no designated smoking area. If you're dealing with cravings, talk to your care team — they may be able to help.

instruction: What accessibility supports are available?
response: LHSC provides drop-off points at main doors for people with mobility challenges, wheelchairs at entrances, amplified phones, relay services, and sign language and deaf-blind translation upon request. All required documents can be provided in accessible formats. If you need accommodations, let your care team know. Accessible parking spaces are available throughout visitor lots and garages.

instruction: What if my family needs accommodations in London?
response: The Ronald McDonald House may be an option for families from outside London — speak with your care team about eligibility. LHSC also maintains a list of local hotels and motels on their website. Some offer preferred hospital rates, so it's worth asking when booking. The hospital doesn't endorse specific accommodations but provides the list as a community service.

instruction: Who can see my health information?
response: Your personal health information can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent to or refuse the collection and sharing of your health information, request access to your records, ask for corrections, and be notified if it's accessed inappropriately. For questions, contact the Privacy Office at extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: What is a care partner vs. a visitor?
response: A care partner is someone more directly involved in supporting your care — like a parent or primary caregiver. Inpatients can have up to two care partners at the bedside at once, while outpatients are limited to one. Care partners currently don't need to register. Visitors are friends, extended family, etc. who come to see you. All visitors must follow infection control rules and check optimal visiting times with unit staff.

instruction: Where's the breast pump room?
response: The breast pump room is in Zone B, 6th floor, room B6-235. Nurses can provide containers and computer-generated labels for breast milk. Labeled containers should be given to the nurse for refrigeration or freezing. Breast pump kits can be purchased at the pharmacy (B1-001).

instruction: What's the Culliton Family Lounge?
response: The Culliton Family Lounge is at B6-110 on the inpatient unit. It's a shared space where patients can hang out, relax, and socialize with family or friends outside of their room. It's also used for group events and family coffee hours.

instruction: What if I have ethical concerns about my care?
response: LHSC has a clinical ethics consultation service. If you or your family are struggling with a difficult ethical decision around your care, the ethicist can help identify and work through those concerns. Ethics consultations are available to patients, families, and health-care providers. More info is on the LHSC website, or ask your care team.

instruction: Can a pharmacist explain my medications to me?
response: Yes. If you have questions about your medications, ask your nurse to contact a pharmacist on your behalf. The pharmacist can come talk to you directly. If you're on several medications, they can also prepare a medication calendar and review it with you before you go home.

instruction: What if I need to go to school while I'm here?
response: The Transitions in Care team helps with the school-to-hospital-to-school transition. Before discharge, it may be useful to speak with your teacher about missed work and your return. On the discharge checklist, the hospital reminds families to discuss conditions and health-care needs with principals or relevant school staff. Your social worker can also help with this.

instruction: What's the Heroes' Circle program?
response: The Heroes' Circle is a year-round program that offers weekly visits for inpatients and clinic patients, including siblings. You learn breathing and relaxation techniques along with martial arts. It's designed to help you feel more in control and cope better during your hospital experience. You can contact them at info@kidskickingcancer.ca.

instruction: Can I get music therapy?
response: Yes. An accredited music therapist at Children's Hospital uses music-based activities to support patients in areas like pain control and rehabilitation. It's available for patients of any age, illness, or disability, and you don't need any musical skill to participate. Ask your care team to arrange a session.

instruction: Is there a place for Indigenous families?
response: The Indigenous Healing Space at E1-204 is open to all, with priority given to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous Peoples accessing care at LHSC and their families. There's also a Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant who supports mental health and cultural wellness. For more information, speak with your care team or email IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Where can I find information about my condition?
response: The Paediatric Family Resource Centre at B1-006 has health information resources and internet access. Online, the hospital recommends AboutKidsHealth (from SickKids), Caring for Kids (from Canada's paediatricians), and MedlinePlus. For questions specific to your care, always ask your care team — they're the best source for your situation.

instruction: How do I contact Patient Relations?
response: You can reach Patient Relations by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca (preferred), by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, through the contact form on the LHSC website, or by mail to 800 Commissioners Road East, PO Box 5010, Stn. B, London ON, N6A 5W9. They check messages Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Try speaking with your care team first, as they may be able to resolve your concern directly.

instruction: What's the deal with poinsettias?
response: Poinsettias are completely banned from LHSC. They contain a compound similar to what's found in rubber latex, which can cause a severe allergic reaction through touch or even inhalation. So especially during the holidays, make sure nobody sends or brings poinsettias to the hospital.

instruction: Can I get a security escort to my car?
response: Yes. Security patrols are available to escort you to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House. Just call Security dispatch at extension 52281. It's a smart move if you're leaving late at night.

instruction: Where are the information desks?
response: Information Desks are staffed from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Friday, and noon to 4:00 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday. Guide volunteers are at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. You can also call the hospital operator at 519-685-8500 and press 0.

instruction: What are visiting hours at Children's Hospital?
response: There aren't strict hospital-wide visiting hours. Visiting times are based on the individual patient's condition, care needs, and wishes, so they can vary between patients and units. Check with the unit staff about the best times. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., family members should stay in the patient's room and let staff know when they're coming and going.

instruction: What do I do if my health gets worse after I go home?
response: Before discharge, make sure you know exactly who to call if your health worsens or you have questions — your care team will go over this with you. You should have written instructions for your care at home. If it's an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest Emergency Department. Don't hesitate to reach out to your care team with concerns, even if they seem small.

instruction: What shared decision making means here?
response: Shared Decision Making at LHSC is a structured process where you and your caregivers work with health-care providers and a Decision Coach to make important care choices together. It combines the best medical evidence with your personal values. It's about making sure you have a real say in decisions about your own care. Ask your care team or visit the LHSC website to learn more.

instruction: Can my grandpa use a wheelchair here?
response: Yes! There are wheelchairs available near the hospital entrances. If your grandpa can't find one, he can ask a staff member or volunteer and they'll help him out. There are also drop-off points at the main doors so someone can let him out close to the entrance and then park the car.

instruction: Where do I check in for my appointment?
response: When you get to the hospital, you go to Patient Registration on the second floor of Zone B. That's right above the main entrance. If you're not sure how to find it, look for the guide volunteers near the B1 entrance or B2 lobby — they're there on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. to help!

instruction: What if I'm scared to walk on the slippery floor?
response: That's totally understandable! The hospital wants to make sure you don't slip, so wear your non-slip socks, slippers, or shoes with good grip. If you need help walking around, press the nurse call button and someone will come to help you. You can also ask for a wheelchair if walking feels too tricky.

instruction: Can I share my toys with the kid in the next bed?
response: It's really nice that you want to share, but in the hospital we don't share toys or personal items between patients. This is to stop germs from spreading. Your toys stay with you, and the other kid has their own things. If you want to play together, a nurse or Child Life Specialist can help figure out a safe way to have fun!

instruction: What if I need hearing aids at the hospital?
response: Definitely bring your hearing aids! The hospital wants you to bring any important medical aids you use, like hearing aids, eyeglasses, braces, or crutches. If you're deaf or hard of hearing, the hospital can also arrange special phone services and sign language interpreters for free. Just ask your care team.

instruction: Where can I make a phone call?
response: You can use your own phone, or the hospital has patient telephones you can use for free to make local and toll-free calls. If you need a private spot to make a call, the quiet rooms on the sixth floor (B6-119 and B6-257) can be used for that. Just check with your nurse first.

instruction: What if we don't have a car seat?
response: All kids have to ride in an approved car seat — it's the law! If you need help making sure your car seat is installed the right way, the hospital's Trauma Program has trained Car Seat Technicians who can check it for you. Your nurse can tell your family how to schedule a car seat check.

instruction: Where can I charge my phone?
response: Your room should have outlets you can use — just bring your own charger. The hospital's WiFi is available for connecting to the internet. If you're having any trouble with WiFi, you can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958 for help.

instruction: What if my family can't afford parking?
response: Parking can add up, especially during a longer stay. Multi-day passes bring the daily cost down significantly — a 30-day pass is $75, working out to $2.50/day. 5- and 10-day passes are also available on request from the parking office in P8, ground floor, Room 105. Your social worker may also be able to help connect your family with financial resources.

instruction: Can I stream Netflix or Disney+ here?
response: Yes. The hospital's patient entertainment site lets you log in to your own streaming accounts. You can also watch live Rogers TV for free. The hospital has WiFi, so as long as you have your login credentials, you should be able to stream content on your phone, tablet, or a laptop available through Child Life Services.

instruction: Where's the ATM?
response: ATMs are located near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors, right next to the vending machines. If you need to pay a bill at the Business Office, that's in Zone D, 3rd floor, Room D3-400.

instruction: What if I need home care after discharge?
response: If you need equipment or services at home after discharge, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator will assess your needs before you leave. If you're already receiving community services, contact the coordinator at extension 52249 before going home. For stays longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required — nursing staff can help facilitate the doctor's referral.

instruction: Can my dad stay AND can I keep my stuffed animal? Those are two different questions.
response: Two questions, two yes answers! Your dad can absolutely stay overnight — there's a recliner or cot in your room for parents who want to stay. And your stuffed animal can absolutely stay with you. Lots of kids bring comfort items from home and nobody here will ever make you get rid of it. Having familiar things with you makes a real difference.

instruction: I need my special blanket from home. It's not a baby thing, it just helps me sleep.
response: There is absolutely nothing baby about having something comforting from home — lots of kids and teenagers use comfort objects and it's completely normal. Ask your parent to bring your blanket as soon as possible. If they're not around right now, your nurse can help you reach them. In the meantime, the hospital has extra blankets and can get you a warm one while you wait.

instruction: I haven't slept properly in five days.
response: Five days of poor sleep is serious and worth raising explicitly with your care team — not just mentioning, but flagging as something that needs to be addressed. Sleep is a core part of recovery and it's not something to push through. Talk to your doctor or nurse: 'I haven't slept properly in five days and it's affecting me — what can we do about it?' There may be adjustable factors (lighting, noise, overnight checks, medications) and there may also be short-term sleep support options. You shouldn't have to just wait it out.

instruction: I want to talk to someone about discharge planning. Who starts that conversation?
response: You can start it, and earlier is better. Ask your nurse or physician: 'Can I meet with someone about discharge planning?' The discharge planning team or a social worker will be assigned to work with you. The conversation covers what you'll need when you go home — follow-up appointments, medications, any home care, limitations on activity, and what the plan is for returning to school. Don't wait until you're being told you're leaving to start this conversation. The earlier you raise it, the more time there is to make sure everything is in place.

instruction: I don't want to eat the hospital food. Can I just not eat?
response: Your body really does need food to help it heal, so completely not eating for a long time isn't something your care team will want. But if you truly can't face the hospital meals, tell your nurse — there are usually alternatives, and your family can bring food from home in many cases. Ask: 'Is there something different I could have instead, or can my family bring food?' If you haven't been hungry at all for a while, that's also worth mentioning because it might be related to how you're feeling or your medication.

instruction: Do I have to stay in my room the whole time or can I at least look out the window somewhere?
response: Whether you can move around depends on your specific care plan, but your nurse can tell you exactly what's allowed. Many kids are able to walk the hallway or visit a common area when their plan permits it. If you specifically want to find a window or a different view, tell your nurse — 'I'd really like to see outside, is there somewhere I can go?' is a completely reasonable request and the team will do what they can to help. Getting a change of scenery, even just a different view, can make a real difference.

instruction: What if I need to pee during the night when no one's watching?
response: Your nurses are always around, even at night — they don't leave or stop watching. If you need to go to the bathroom, press your call button and a nurse will come help you. If you have an IV or any tubes attached, they'll unhook what's needed and make sure you can get to the bathroom safely. Never try to get up by yourself in the night if you have tubes or wires, because you could pull something out. Press the button first — your nurse would rather come to you than have you try to manage alone.

instruction: I need to exercise every day but I can't, and now everything feels worse.
response: Movement and exercise are legitimate mental and physical health needs, and losing access to them during a hospital stay is a real loss, not a minor inconvenience. Talk to your care team specifically about this: 'Exercise is important to my mental health and I need some form of movement.' A physiotherapist can suggest appropriate activity given your current situation. Even light movement — stretching, walking the hallway — can help. If the inability to exercise is significantly affecting your mood or mental state, framing it as a health issue (not just a preference) is more likely to get a useful response.

instruction: I think the nurse got something wrong but I'm not sure.
response: It's always okay to mention something that doesn't seem right — and you should. You can say 'I'm not sure, but I thought you said something different earlier' or 'That looks different from what I remember.' Your nurses and doctors actually want to catch any mix-ups before they matter, and they won't be upset that you asked. There are lots of checks in place to catch mistakes, and you speaking up is another layer of safety. It's the right thing to do.

instruction: Is there a way to make it so the light doesn't flash when the IV beeps? It's keeping me up.
response: That's a really reasonable thing to ask about. The alarms on IV pumps can be adjusted or silenced by nursing staff when they've been addressed — your nurse can reset the pump so it's not alarming continuously, and if a particular setting is consistently waking you, they may be able to adjust monitoring intervals or position equipment differently. Tell your nurse: 'The IV alarm light is keeping me awake — is there anything you can do?' Sleep is part of recovering, and they'll take that seriously.

instruction: No one asked me which arm was my good arm before they put the IV in.
response: That's worth mentioning now so it's documented for future procedures. Some people have a preference because of previous experiences, a more accessible vein, or just personal comfort. Tell your nurse: 'I have a preferred arm for things like IVs — can that be noted in my chart?' Once it's in your chart, future staff will see it. If the current IV site is uncomfortable and you'd rather have it moved, that's also worth raising — just ask whether it could be placed differently.

instruction: I keep getting woken up for tests. Can't they do them all at once?
response: That's a completely understandable frustration and worth raising. Ask your nurse: 'Is it possible to cluster my tests and checks so I'm not being woken up as often?' In many cases, nursing staff can coordinate with the lab and other teams to batch certain things together. Not every test has that flexibility — some require specific timing — but the request is reasonable and your care team can tell you which things can be combined and which can't. Sleep matters for your recovery and your team should want to protect it where possible.
